summary: The article argues that After-Action Reviews (AARs) are valuable for improving emergency response but often fail to produce real change because findings are not implemented. Using the September 4, 2023 citywide power outage as a case study, it covers gaps found in the response, criticism from responders and IT staff, and calls for implementation plans, public accountability and leadership commitment. It concludes that AARs are only a starting point and are effective only if their findings are acted on.
one_line: After-Action Reviews can improve emergency response, but the September 2023 power outage shows they fail without committed implementation, accountability and leadership.
key_facts: An After-Action Review (AAR) is a structured review process that helps organizations learn from direct experience, ideally shortly after an event ends and involving all stakeholders.
Military organizations have long used AARs to evaluate exercises and operations, and civilian industries, especially utilities and service sectors, have adopted them.
The citywide power outage began on September 4, 2023, at approximately 3:22 PM on a Tuesday, as children were being dismissed from school and rush hour was starting.
The outage lasted 48 hours, causing traffic lights to fail, the internet to go offline and businesses to halt.
Emergency services were hampered by communication breakdowns, an issue supposedly addressed after a smaller outage the previous year.
The AAR, convened by the local utility company with emergency services, community leaders and affected businesses, was led by crisis management expert Dr. Simon Torres.
Dr. Torres' initial findings identified inadequate backup power sources, underestimation of cascading effects, and a lack of coordination between emergency support functions.
Veteran paramedic Alex Jennings said, "We go through these reviews, talk a good game about changing protocols, but when it comes down to the wire, we fall back on old habits."
IT specialist Jennifer Martin said there is a disconnect between strategic decisionmakers and operational staff, so proposed changes are impractical or ignored in the field.
Advocates say AARs need a realistic implementation plan that sets priorities, delegates responsibilities, sets deadlines, and is regularly monitored and flexible.
Mayor Andrea Bishop promised ongoing public briefings on AAR progress and steps toward implementing recommended revisions.
A cyberattack on the national telecommunications provider on November 10, 2023 showed that crises are unpredictable, supporting the need for flexible, adaptive plans.
Obstacles to implementation include the inertia of existing systems, budget constraints and political considerations.
